### Option 2: Elegant Literary Prose
*Best if you prefer a continuous narrative paragraph suitable for a prose poem, essay, or historical reflection.*

> Dating to the Mithridatic Wars of the first century BC, our general remained elsewhere while we met our end beneath the waves. While he rested, he dispatched us home laden with the heavy spoils that had long burdened his army. A thrashing storm overtook us, shattering our hulls and delivering us as offerings to the sea floor—a cascading rain of statues, gold, and men. 
> 
> Relieved at last from service and finished with war, as the crash and hiss of the surface faded into silence, we drifted down through currents of marine life—creatures existing simply for the quiet purpose of living. We came to rest alongside treasures plundered from the ruined temples of Athenian Greece. Among our ranks lay gods and goddesses of bronze and marble, awkwardly grounded on the seabed and casually bypassed by incurious fish. 
> 
> Their divine power was never meant to save us, and our earthly pleasures were merely incidental gifts; yet, awestruck by their radiance within our mortal dust, we had given them our voices. Now, their sculpted faces, wings, and limbs lie entangled with our sand-worn bones and rusted, motionless implements. Small crabs endeavor to adorn themselves with our rings of agate and amethyst, and many an octopus, seeking a quiet hour of rest, finds sanctuary within our hollow skulls. 
>

outputs.L2:
Here is a complete prose rewrite of the passage, retaining all original details while using distinct phrasing and structure:

During the Mithridatic conflicts of the first century BC, our military leader remained behind to rest, ordering us to sail home ahead of him. We carried the immense weight of plunder that had previously burdened his marching troops. Our commander was not present when a violent tempest struck, splintering the frames of our vessels and casting us into the watery deep. A deluge of soldiers, precious metals, and sculpted figures plummeted to the ocean floor. 

With our combat duties forcefully concluded, the roaring chaos of the storm faded away. We drifted downward through underwater currents filled with marine creatures living out their natural existences. We eventually settled on the seabed alongside sacred riches stolen from the ruined shrines of Athens. Among our ranks lay ungraceful stone and metal representations of male and female deities, which indifferent sea life simply navigated around. 

The divine powers of these idols were never intended to save us from drowning, for human happiness was merely an incidental concern to them. Yet, overwhelmed by their brilliant majesty within our fleeting earthly lives, we had once granted them our devotion and prayers. 

Today, the sculpted faces, wings, and limbs of these deities are scattered across the sand alongside our worn skeletons and broken equipment. Small crabs attempt to crawl into jewelry set with amethyst and agate, while weary octopuses retreat inside our empty skulls to sleep. Even in death, our remains serve a purpose.
outputs.L3:
In the tempestuous first century BC, amidst the brutal violence of the Mithridatic Wars, a warship laden with the heavy spoils of conquest met a violent end. Homeward-bound soldiers, exhausted from years of campaign, steered their vessel through treacherous waters, its hold weighed down by priceless treasures looted from the sacred sanctuaries of Greece. Yet, the triumph of victory was swiftly erased by the sea. A sudden, violent storm tore through the ship, shattering its timbers and dragging the crew, their stolen fortunes, and their grand ambitions into the dark abyssal depths.

As the shattered vessel rested on the cold ocean floor, a quiet, mournful scene played out in the dark. The drowned crew settled into the seabed alongside the very treasures they had died to possess—stolen bronze and marble statues depicting the great gods and goddesses of the ancient world. For generations, mortals had offered sacrifices, built temples, and poured out desperate devotion to these divine figures, begging for safety and favor. Yet, submerged in the quiet deep, a stark reality emerged: the gods were entirely indifferent, as powerless against the indiscriminate wrath of the ocean as the men who had worshiped them. 

As decades turned into centuries, the tragedy of the wreck faded into the timeless rhythm of the deep ocean, giving way to a strange and vibrant renewal. Marine life slowly claimed the site of human loss. Octopuses crept into the hollowed brain-cases of human skulls, finding safe, dark shelters in the former chambers of thought. Hermit crabs scurried across the sea floor, decorating their shells with glittering, long-forgotten jewels, while sea anemones and coral draped themselves over the serene, frozen faces of the marble deities. 

Though the lives of the soldiers ended in terror and defeat, their drowned remains and the artifacts of a fallen empire were not lost to meaninglessness. Stripped of their context of war, greed, and divine pretense, the relics of the ancient world were granted an enduring, quiet rebirth. In the silence of the abyss, human tragedy and imperial ambition were repurposed, serving forever as a sanctuary for the humble creatures of the sea.
outputs.L4:
The sun dipped below the horizon, casting a bruised, purple hue across the waters of the Aegean. In the wake of Sulla’s brutal sack of Athens during the First Mithridatic War, a heavy Roman transport ship pushed out into the open sea, her timber frame straining beneath a immense, suffocating weight. Her hold was crammed with the stolen splendor of Classical Greece: priceless bronze deities stripped from their pedestals, hand-carved marble friezes, gold vessels, and heavy chests of coin. Alongside these sacred relics sat rows of legionnaires and sailors, weary from siege and drunk on the prospect of the immense wealth waiting for them in Rome. 

They had barely cleared the treacherous coastal capes when the sky turned black as iron. Without warning, a sudden, ferocious tempest tore through the night, unleashing howling winds and mountain-sized waves. The ship was tossed violently in the churn. Below deck, the great bronze gods—once worshipped in quiet, incense-filled sanctuaries—shifted against the hull like restless giants, their immense weight battering the wooden beams from within. Sailors screamed over the roar of the gale, frantically trying to heave cargo into the sea, but the sheer weight of their plunder doomed them. A titanic wave broke over the main deck, shattering the mainmast and snapping the ship's spine. 

In a violent rush of foam, splintered oak, and rushing water, the ship went down. Men and gods plunged together into the icy black depths. Soldiers weighed down by their iron mail sank like stones, their final gasps swallowed by the sea, falling alongside the serene, unblinking faces of Apollo and Athena. Down, down they drifted through the water column, leaving the chaos of the howling storm behind, descending into a realm of absolute, sunless silence.

When they finally struck the ocean bed, the sea floor absorbed the impact in a cloud of fine, soft silt. The storm above eventually subsided, leaving the wreckage undisturbed in the deep.

Centuries rolled past in the dark, and the violent ambitions of men were slowly erased by time. The iron armor of the legionnaires rusted away, and the wood of the vessel dissolved into the sea, but the artifacts and the skeletons remained. Nature, patient and indifferent to the wars of mankind, claimed the wreckage. 

Over generations, the cold seabed transformed the site of tragedy into a thriving, hidden oasis. Vibrant pink coral wrapped itself around the marble limbs of fallen heroes, and sea anemones bloomed like delicate flowers across the bronze brows of forgotten gods. Barnacles encrusted the sacred vessels, turning them into shimmering, textured relics. The hollow ribcages of the long-drowned soldiers became safe nurseries for small, translucent shrimp, while octopuses made their lairs within the bellies of shattered amphorae. What had once been forged for divine worship and stolen through human greed had found a quiet, unintended immortality—offering shelter, color, and life to the gentle creatures of the deep.
outputs.L5:
**Title: Echoes of Pontus: The Legacy of the Mithridatic Wars**

In the first century BCE, the Mediterranean world was violently reshaped by a series of three devastating conflicts that tested the ultimate resilience of the late Roman Republic. Fought between 88 and 63 BCE, these clashes pitted the disciplined legions of Rome against Mithridates VI, the ambitious king of Pontus, a brilliant ruler renowned for his cunning, multilingual diplomacy, and legendary immunity to poisons. 

The catalyst for the struggle was Mithridates’ desire to unite the Hellenistic East and liberate Asia Minor from the heavy tax burdens and iron grip of Roman rule. In 88 BCE, he orchestrated a brutal, coordinated massacre known as the "Asiatic Vespers," in which an estimated 80,000 Roman and Italian civilians were slaughtered in a single day. This atrocity made conflict inevitable and thrust Rome into a quarter-century of bitter warfare across Anatolia, Greece, and the Black Sea region.

Over the course of three distinct wars, Rome dispatched its most capable—and power-hungry—generals to crush the Pontic threat. Lucius Cornelius Sulla dealt the initial blow, defeating Pontic forces in Greece before being forced to negotiate a hasty treaty due to political rivalries back home. Years later, Lucius Licinius Lucullus waged a brilliant campaign of attrition that shattered Mithridates’ main armies. Finally, Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus (Pompey the Great) delivered the decisive stroke, driving the aging king to the far reaches of the Crimea, where Mithridates ultimately took his own life in 63 BCE.

**From** the mountain fortresses of Pontus to the political corridors of the Roman Senate, the fallout **from** the **Mithridatic** **Wars** fundamentally altered the course of Western history. 

Territorially, Rome’s victory transformed the Eastern Mediterranean. Vast areas of Asia Minor, Syria, and Judea were converted into Roman provinces or client states, channeling unprecedented wealth and trade routes into the Republic. However, the domestic costs were immense. The extraordinary military commands granted to generals like Sulla and Pompey eroded traditional Republican norms, creating ultra-wealthy, fiercely loyal armies dependent on their individual commanders rather than the state. 

Ultimately, the triumph over Mithridates set off a domino effect. The immense power gained by commanders during these campaigns destabilized the Senate, accelerating the civil wars that would soon destroy the Republic and give rise to the Roman Empire. Though Mithridates was eventually defeated, his relentless resistance forever transformed the empire he had sought to destroy.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an atmospheric free verse poem from the collective perspective ("we") of sailors who drowned during the Mithridatic Wars while transporting looted Greek statues and treasures. Include imagery of marine life interacting with the sunken wreckage.
counterfactuals.output:
We sank beneath the weight of stolen gods.

Our timber groaned under marble thighs and bronze breasts—
towers of chiseled Olympus packed in the hold,
snatched from the temples of Athens and Delos
to pave the grand parades of Rome.
When the gale broke the spine of our galley,
the sea did not care for Sulla’s triumph.
We went down together into the sunless green:
the living, the dead, and the immortal.

Now we rest in the cold, silted darkness
where daylight dies in thin, blue threads.
Here, Lord Apollo sits half-buried in sand,
his carved toes wrapped in waving eel-grass,
his blank stone eyes staring at the endless drift.

The ocean has rewritten the plunder.
A soft-bodied octopus has made its den
within the hollow chest of a bronze hero,
its dark tentacles pulsing through the gap in the breastplate
like smoke from a forgotten altar.
Barnacles crown the helm of Athena;
crustaceans weave through her marble hair,
building tiny, calcified cities upon the goddess of wisdom.

Spilled from shattered amphorae,
silver coins glitter among the purple sea-urchins,
useless wealth for the shoals of darting minnows
that flash like tossed blades through our shattered ribs.
Small crabs scuttle across the white curves of our skulls,
indifferent to the wars of Mithridates,
blind to the borders of emperors and kings.

We were only the men who pulled the oars,
drowned in the shadow of looted grace.
Now, a school of silver fish glides silently
through the parted lips of a stone nymph
who was carved to sing of victory,

while we, in the suffocating quiet,
drift into the coral,
and become part of the reef.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about the Antikythera shipwreck from the viewpoint of the drowned crew resting on the ocean floor alongside marble gods and broken mechanisms.
counterfactuals.output:
We rest in the turquoise twilight’s crush,
Where the roaring storm is a forgotten sigh.
Our oak has rotted, our sails are dust,
Beneath the weight of a wine-dark sky.
The Aegean drew us down to sleep,
Two hundred fathoms beneath the foam,
And built us a court in the silent deep,
Where flesh and marble have made a home.

Beside our ribcages, gods of stone
Lie half-entombed in the shifting sand.
Great Herakles rests on a bed of bone,
A broken club in his barnacled hand.
And Hermes stares with his blank, carved eyes
Into the black where no sun can gleam;
Divinity divested of its skies,
Drowned like men in a motionless dream.

And here, where our calcified fingers touch,
Lies the miraculous, rusted chest—
A mass of bronze in the salt’s cold clutch,
Its secrets locked in a frozen rest.
With calculated, intricate teeth,
It traced the stars in their celestial dance,
Predicting the moons that would rise beneath,
Unaware of our sudden, fatal chance.

It knew the path of the sun’s bright car,
The dark eclipse and the planetary line,
Yet could not foretell a hidden bar,
Or the violent will of the sea’s design.
Its bronze heart corrodes into verdigris,
Its gears jammed fast by the ocean’s grime—
A metal mind swallowed by the sea,
Trapping the cosmos, trapping time.

How strange a court we have gathered here:
The forgotten crew, the gods, the gear.
The stone loses shape as the centuries creep,
Our marrow turns into coral and lime,
While the machine keeps the silence of the deep,
No longer bound to the ticks of time.

Let the world above us turn and spin,
Searching the heavens for chart and guide.
We hold the universe trapped within
This quiet grave where the currents glide.
Together we lie in the lightless deep—
The bronze, the marble, the drowned, the dust—
Guarding the stars in an endless sleep,
Bound by the salt and the slow-eating rust.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Adopt the persona of the forgotten soldiers who perished carrying Sulla's plunder from Athenian Greece in the 1st century BC. Write a quiet, melancholic poem exploring their afterlife on the seabed as sea creatures make homes in their bones and jewelry.
counterfactuals.output:
The gale was heavy with the weight of stolen gods,
Of marble knees and gold from sacred halls.
When Sulla turned his back to march on Rome,
He left us in the dark where no sun falls.
The timber groaned beneath the Athenian freight,
And dragged us down—a quiet, heavy fate.

Two hundred fathoms deep, the storm is hushed.
The iron rots from breastplate and from spear.
Our names were washed away before the tide
Could carry word to those who held us dear.
We have no graves of stone, no mournful pyre,
Only the slow, blue sleep of salt and mire.

Where once my fingers clutched a leather rein,
A hermit crab now claims a signet ring;
It crawls through rusted links of mail to hide
Beneath the silver chalice of a king.
Small pale anemones, like ghost-flowers, bloom
Along the quiet scaffolding of my spine.

My comrade lies beside a shattered amphora,
His open ribs a cage where seahorses rest;
A drift of tarnished drachmas from Piraeus
Is piled like shining sand across his chest.
An octopus glides through his iron helm,
Soft-bodied, soft-eyed, sovereign of this realm.

We carried Greece away in bronze and gold,
To pay for battles fought on Roman soil—
Yet all the wealth of Delphi could not buy
A single breath to pay us for our toil.
The gods we stole now sleep beside our bones,
Turned back to harmless, silent, water-smoothed stones.

No triumph waits for us in paved Rome’s streets.
No laurel wreath shall touch these seaweed strands.
Yet it is peaceful here, beneath the waves,
Far from the iron boots, the blood-soaked lands.
The sea is gentle with the things we kept:
It wears our gold, and guards us while we sleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poem about ancient Roman or Greek shipwrecks? Make it haunting and peaceful, focusing on the contrast between majestic looted statues, human remains, and ocean life like crabs and octopuses.
counterfactuals.output:
Beneath three thousand years of sunless blue,
Where Mediterranean currents softly creep,
The shattered hull of pine and resinous yew
Rests in the cradles of the silent deep.

Here lie the gods, the plundered art of Greece,
In marble cold and bronze refined by fire—
Once dragged away to grace a Roman hall,
Now held in endless, serene release,
Divorced from human triumph and desire,
Beyond the reach of empire or of fall.

An octopus, fluid and ghost-like, weaves
Through the cracked visor of a hero’s helm,
And makes its dark house in Apollo's brow,
Where coral blooms like pale, forgotten leaves.
A quiet sovereign in a submerged realm,
It claims the fallen sky-god's temple now.

Across a sculpted emperor’s marble thigh,
Slow spider crabs in strange procession tread,
Their needle legs tracing the chiseled folds,
Indifferent to the power long gone by.
They scavenge on the threshold of the dead,
Where silt and sea-salt turn the bronze to golds.

And in the shadow of a shattered urn,
A sailor's ribcage rests in drifted sand,
Pale ivory softened by the salt and tide.
No storm remains to make the timber turn,
No captain calls, no crew to seek the land;
The terror of the wreck has gently died.

Small glass-fish drift through hollowed pelvic bone,
While sea-anemones like stars unfold
Upon a stern-post carved with ancient grace.
The sea forgives the iron and the stone,
The lost ambition and the stolen gold,
And lulls them all in its immense embrace.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short poem set during the Mithridatic Wars about a ship sinking with stolen treasure.
counterfactuals.output:
Heavy with the plunder of the conquered Pontic coast,  
The warship bore the riches that a Consul prized the most:  
Gilded gods of Delos, chalices of gold,  
And silver from the temples in her overflowing hold.  

The Black Sea rose in fury, dark as Mithridates' hate,  
The timber groaned and splintered beneath the gilded weight.  
No Roman oar could save her as the salt waves rushed inside,  
Plunging all the spoils of war beneath the churning tide.  

Down sank the heavy coin, down sank the stolen grace,  
To rest forever silent in the ocean's cold embrace.  
While kings and legions battled for a fleeting earthly fame,  
The deep sea kept the treasure—and forgot the victor's name.
